unit.title: Other assets
unit.description: SOCIMIs, derivatives, CFDs, pension plans and where to keep short-term money

u11l1.title: Property on the stock market: SOCIMIs and REITs

texts: Your own flat or a SOCIMI?
You have €500 and want to invest in property. A **SOCIMI** (in the US, a **REIT**) is a listed company with offices, warehouses or homes for rent: your own flat or a SOCIMI?
Your own flat
SOCIMI
You need tens of thousands of euros up front
Buying a flat takes a lot of money in one go.
You can sell in seconds
It's listed on the stock market: you sell whenever you like.
You spread your money across many properties
Offices, warehouses, shopping centres… in a single share.
You find the tenant and fix the boiler
With your own flat, managing it is down to you.
Its price changes every day
It's listed, so it can fall like the stock market.
Pays out most of its profit in dividends
In exchange for paying very little corporation tax: that's why its dividends are usually high.
Sort all six features.
With a SOCIMI you buy its shares on the stock market and own a slice of lots of buildings, **with little money** and the option to sell in seconds. What you can't avoid is its price moving every day.
Hint: is it listed on the stock market, or do you have to manage it yourself?
Sort each feature
Bricks and mortar falling?
Bruno
Interest rates shoot up and SOCIMIs fall 25 %.
How can something with buildings behind it fall that much?
What do you explain to him?
That this shouldn't happen with property
It does: they borrow to buy and, with high rates, borrowing costs more.
That they're sensitive to rates: it's part of their risk
That's it! Their debt costs more and bonds compete with their dividends.
That he should sell now, just in case
If he knew the risk when he bought, better to decide based on his plan than on the scare.
Knowing an asset's risks in advance helps you not to react in the heat of the moment.

steps.title: Pros and risks
steps.body:
A SOCIMI must pay out at least **80 %** of the profit that comes from rents; a US REIT, at least **90 %** of its taxable profit.

Risks: they're listed and **can fall like the stock market**, they suffer when rates rise (they borrow and compete with bonds) and they depend on their sector, like offices after the pandemic.
steps.key: A SOCIMI is bricks and mortar that trades on the market: diversified and liquid, but with stock-market volatility.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, search for Merlin Properties, a SOCIMI in the IBEX 35, and look at its chart in monthly candles.

u11l2.title: Futures and options in one lesson

texts: Tomás's wheat
Tomás
Tomás is a farmer. He'll harvest his wheat in six months' time.
Today wheat is at a good price. What if it's dropped by the time he harvests?
What can he do with futures?
Sell futures today and lock in the price of his wheat
Hedging! If the price falls, the future makes up for it; if it rises, he gives up that gain.
Buy wheat futures to profit if it rises
That doubles his bet that wheat goes up: the opposite of hedging.
Nothing: futures are only for speculating
They were invented precisely to cover risks like his.
A **future** binds both sides: a future date, a price agreed today.
Obligation or right?
An **option** gives the right, but not the obligation, to buy (**call**) or sell (**put**) at an agreed price, the **strike**. You pay a **premium** for that right.
Has an obligation
Only has a right
Whoever buys a future
In a future, both sides are obliged to go through with it.
Whoever buys a call
A call gives the right to buy at the strike. If it doesn't suit them, they don't use it.
Whoever sells a future
Also obliged: a future binds both sides.
Whoever buys a put
A put gives the right to sell at the strike.
Whoever sells an option and collects the premium
They collect the premium and take on the obligation if the buyer exercises it.
Sort all five cases.
A future **binds** both sides. An option gives a **right** to whoever buys it, in exchange for a premium; whoever sells it takes on the obligation.
Hint: whoever pays the premium gets to choose.
Sort each case
Your call, at expiry
You buy a **call** with a **€100** strike and pay a **€5** premium. At expiry, do you win or lose?
You win
You lose
The share ends at €130
You buy at €100 something worth €130: €30 minus the €5 premium, you make €25.
The share ends at €80
Buying at €100 makes no sense: you don't exercise it and lose the premium, €5.
The share ends at €103
You exercise and make €3, but you paid a €5 premium: you lose €2.
The share ends at €150
150 − 100 − 5 = €45 profit per share.
The share crashes to €50
Even if it crashes, you only lose the premium: €5.
Work out all five endings.
With a bought option you win if the price beats **strike + premium** (here, €105), and the most you can lose is the **premium**. Whoever sold it to you, on the other hand, can lose much more.
Hint: below €105 you don't get the premium back.
Do you win or lose in each ending?

steps.title: Why they're not for beginners
steps.body:
Futures and options are **derivatives**: their value depends on another asset. With a future you only put down **margin**, a fraction of the value: that's leverage.

A small move turns into a big gain or loss and, in some cases (selling options, futures), you can lose more than you put in. If you can't explain how much you could lose in the worst case, don't trade derivatives.
steps.key: Future = an obligation at an agreed price. Option = a right in exchange for a premium.
steps.tip: Try it: on your next purchase in the simulator, set a stop: it limits your loss without using derivatives.

texts: A 5 % that wipes everything out
An ad invites you to trade **CFDs** «at 20 to 1». With a CFD you receive or pay the price difference of an asset, **with leverage**: you put down margin and move a much bigger position.
You put in €1,000 with 20 to 1 leverage. What price drop wipes out all your margin?
A 50 % one
A 20 % one
A 5 % one
At 20 to 1 you control **€20,000**, and 5 % of €20,000 is exactly your €1,000: 100 % ÷ 20 = 5 %.
At ×20, find the drop that wipes out your margin.
Leverage **multiplies** the move: at ×20, a 5 % move against you takes 100 % of your margin. A normal move over a few weeks can wipe it out.
Margin gone. And the broker closes the position.
A small move, a huge bite.
It multiplies the gains… and the losses too.
Raise the leverage and move the price
Why most people lose
Simulation: 1,000 people trade CFDs **with no edge at all**, like flipping a coin. Each trade costs **€5** in spread and financing.
Increase the trades until 3 in 4 are losing.
With no edge, the costs of each trade mean most people lose. In real life, according to the CNMV's mandatory warning, **between 74 and 89 %** of retail investors lose money with CFDs.
Three in four losing. And nobody did any worse than anyone else.
Look at the average: every trade chips a bit off it.
Increase each person's trades

steps.title: What the EU requires
steps.body:
A CFD doesn't give you the asset: it's a contract with your broker for the **price difference**. And you pay **financing** for every night the position stays open.

Maximum leverage for retail investors in the EU: 30 to 1 on major currencies, 20 to 1 on major indices and gold, 5 to 1 on shares and **2 to 1 on crypto**. And every broker must display the CNMV's warning, alongside its own percentage: «CFDs are complex instruments and come with a high risk of losing money rapidly due to leverage». In Spain, advertising CFDs to the public has been banned since August 2023: if you see an ad, that is already a warning sign.
steps.key: Leverage multiplies gains and, above all, losses: most retail investors lose money with CFDs.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open the gold chart in weekly candles and think about what ×20 would do to your margin each week.

texts: A plan «for the tax relief»
Ana
Ana is 23 and has just got her first salary. Her IRPF marginal rate is low.
The bank is offering me a pension plan «for the tax relief». It charges 1.5 % a year.
What do you tell her?
Tax relief always pays off
With a low rate, she saves little. And she'd pay 1.5 % a year for decades.
It depends on her marginal rate, the fees and whether she'll need the money
That's it! It pays off with a high rate today, low fees and money you won't need.
She won't pay tax when she cashes it in
She will: everything she cashes in is taxed as employment income.
A pension plan isn't good or bad in general: it depends on your situation.
The small print
What you pay into a **pension plan** cuts your IRPF (Spanish income tax) today, but there's small print. Advantage or drawback?
Advantage
Drawback
Cuts your IRPF in the year you pay in
Up to €1,500 a year in a personal plan.
The money is locked away for years
You can only cash it in at retirement or in specific cases.
When you cash it in, it's all taxed as employment income
Contributions and gains, at your marginal rate at that time.
Gains aren't taxed while it stays invested
The money grows tax-free until you cash it in.
High fees on many bank plans
Check them: they can eat up the tax advantage.
Sort all five features.
You get tax relief going in, the money grows tax-free and **you pay on the way out**. Whether it's worth it depends on your marginal rate, the fees and when you'll need the money.
Hint: think about today, the years of waiting and cashing it in.
Sort each feature

steps.title: Tax relief today, tax tomorrow
steps.body:
Paying into a personal plan reduces your taxable income by up to **€1,500 a year** (up to €10,000 in total with contributions to workplace plans). With a 30 % marginal rate, paying in €1,500 saves you **€450** that year.

You can only cash it in at retirement, in specific cases (long-term unemployment, serious illness, disability, dependency) or for contributions more than **10 years** old. It pays off mainly if your rate is high today and you expect it to be lower when you retire. And check the fees: the plan doesn't save you those.
steps.key: A pension plan defers tax and locks your money away: useful if you pay a lot of IRPF today.
steps.tip: Try it: ask Lumi, your teacher, whether a pension plan would pay off with your salary today.

u11l5.title: Deposits, savings accounts and money market funds

texts: And what does it buy?
You have **€10,000** in a deposit paying **2.5 %**. Inflation is at **2.7 %**.
Do you gain purchasing power with that deposit?
Yes: 2.5 % a year
No: you lose a tiny bit every year
It depends on the bank
2.5 − 2.7 ≈ **−0.2 %** a year: in 10 years you'll have €12,801, which will buy what €9,807 buys today.
With that inflation, find what it would have to pay for you to earn 1 % real.

To earn 1 % real with 2.7 % inflation, the deposit would have to pay almost **3.75 %**, and that's before the 19 % withholding tax. These products are for **keeping money safe**, not for getting rich.
Your balance goes up, but it buys a little less each year.
You're not losing any more. Keep going up a bit more.
Raise what the deposit pays
Is it covered by the FGD?
The **Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos** (FGD, Spain's deposit guarantee scheme) covers up to **€100,000** per holder and per bank if a bank goes bust. What does it cover?
Yes, up to €100,000
No
Current account
It's money deposited in a bank.
12-month deposit
Covered up to €100,000 per holder and per bank.
Money market fund
It's an investment fund: no FGD, but its assets are kept separate from the management company.
Shares in a bank
They're an investment, not a deposit.
Interest-bearing account
Money deposited in a bank: covered.
A stablecoin
The FGD covers bank deposits, not crypto-assets.
Sort all six products.
The FGD covers money **deposited in banks**, not investments. A money market fund isn't covered, but its risk is very low (not zero) and, as a fund, it can be **transferred** without paying tax.
Hint: is it a bank deposit or an investment?
Sort each product
Bruno's cushion
Bruno
I want a €6,000 cushion for emergencies. I'm torn between three options.
A 3-year deposit with a penalty for cancelling, an interest-bearing account with no lock-in, or an equity ETF.
Which suits a cushion best?
The 3-year deposit, which pays a bit more
If an emergency comes up, cancelling it will cost him the penalty.
The interest-bearing account with no lock-in
Nice! Available instantly, covered by the FGD and with a bit of interest.
The equity ETF, which returns more
In a crisis it could fall 30 % just when he needs it most.
A cushion isn't there to earn: it's there to be there when you need it.

steps.title: Three places for the short term
steps.body:
• **Interest-bearing account:** pays interest and you take your money out whenever you like. Watch out for limits: sometimes it only pays on up to a certain amount or for a few months.
• **Fixed-term deposit:** you lock your money away for a while at a fixed rate.
• **Money market fund:** very short-term, high-quality debt; its return follows ECB rates.

Always compare the **APR** and the terms. They're for your emergency cushion and what you'll need within months or a few years, not for the long term.
steps.key: Short term: access and safety before returns.
steps.tip: Try it: open your Portfolio and see how much virtual money you have uninvested: it's your cushion in the simulator.

u11l1-6.prompt: With a SOCIMI you can invest in property with far less money than buying a flat.

u11l1-10.prompt: What are the risks of investing in a SOCIMI? Select all.
options: Its sector doing badly (empty offices, for example)
Its price falling with the stock market
u11l1-10.explanation: The SOCIMI manages the properties; you take on market, interest-rate and sector risks.

u11l1-11.prompt: You have €300 and want to invest in Spanish property. Which option makes sense?
options: Waiting until you have enough for a deposit on a flat
A platform promising a guaranteed 15 % on flats
Buying shares in a SOCIMI in the IBEX 35, like Merlin Properties
u11l1-11.explanation: A SOCIMI lets you invest in property with little money, diversified and with liquidity, in exchange for its price moving every day. A guaranteed return is tempting, but in investing it doesn't exist.
feedback: It could be a goal, but it would take years and you'd have everything in a single property.
Nobody can guarantee 15 %: it's the typical promise of a scam.
Good: with little money you own part of many buildings and can sell whenever you like.

options: Yes, and they're covered by the FGD too
No: the dividend isn't guaranteed and the price can fall like the stock market
u11l1-12.explanation: A SOCIMI is a share: it pays out a lot because the law requires it, but its dividend depends on rents and its price is listed. Comparing it with a deposit is tempting because of the dividend, but it has no fixed interest and no FGD.
feedback: The FGD covers bank deposits, not shares.
It depends on rental profits: it can go down.
That's it. And the FGD doesn't cover shares.
lines: So they're like a deposit, but better?

u11l2-1.prompt: Match each term to its definition.
u11l2-1.explanation: The key difference: a future obliges you; a bought option only gives you a right.
right: Right to sell at an agreed price
What you pay for an option
Right to buy at an agreed price
Obligation to buy or sell on a date at an agreed price

u11l2-2.prompt: An option gives you the ____, but not the obligation, to buy or sell.
u11l2-2.explanation: That's why the buyer pays a premium: they're free not to use it.

u11l2-3.prompt: An option to buy is called a ____.
u11l2-3.explanation: A put is the option to sell; the strike is the agreed price.

u11l2-5.prompt: With the same call (strike €100, premium €5), at expiry the share is worth €95. How much do you lose per share?
u11l2-5.explanation: There's no point buying for €100 something worth €95: you don't exercise it and you lose the premium, €5.

u11l2-7.prompt: Marta sees someone on social media who «makes thousands a month selling options» and wants to try it with her savings. What should she bear in mind?
options: That selling options is collecting easy premiums with no risk
That by selling options she can lose far more than she collects, and that she should understand it first without real money
That if it's on social media, it's been proven
u11l2-7.explanation: Whoever sells an option collects a little and takes on a risk that can be huge.
feedback: You collect small premiums many times… until a sharp move makes you lose far more than you've taken in.
Good: selling a call without owning the share has, in theory, unlimited losses.
Social media shows the gains, rarely the losses.

options: You sell calls without owning the share to collect the premium
You own shares and buy a put in case they fall
Someone with no shares buys calls to profit if the market rises
An airline buys oil futures to lock in what it will pay for fuel
A farmer sells futures on his harvest
u11l2-11.explanation: Hedging means using the derivative to reduce a risk you already have: fuel, the harvest, your shares. If you didn't have that risk before, the derivative protects you from nothing: it's a bet, and selling calls without the share can turn out very expensive.
right: Hedges a risk they already have

u11l3-4.prompt: According to the CNMV's mandatory warning, between 74 and 89 % of retail investors lose money with CFDs.
u11l3-4.explanation: It's the figure from ESMA's 2018 intervention, which every broker must display alongside its own percentage.

u11l3-6.prompt: In the EU, a retail investor can trade crypto CFDs with 100 to 1 leverage.
u11l3-6.explanation: The maximum for retail investors on crypto is 2 to 1.

u11l3-7.prompt: Select the messages that are a warning sign or a scam.
options: «I'm your personal account manager. Deposit €250 and I'll trade for you with 1:500 leverage.»
«Copy my CFD trades: 95 % win rate guaranteed.»
«Multiply your money x50 with gold CFDs. No risk. Limited places.»
«Warning: between 74 and 89 % of retail investor accounts lose money with CFDs.»
u11l3-7.explanation: Returns «with no risk», leverage banned for retail investors in the EU, «account managers» who message you and guaranteed wins are classic signs of an unauthorised firm.

u11l3-8.prompt: Why do most retail investors lose money with CFDs?
options: Leverage turns small moves into big losses, and there are costs every night on top
Because they can only be traded in the early hours
u11l3-8.explanation: Leverage, financing costs and heat-of-the-moment decisions: a combination that hits beginners hardest.

u11l3-10.prompt: Pablo opened a leveraged CFD and he's losing. The broker warns him that his margin has fallen to half of what's required. What happens if it keeps falling?
options: The broker gives him back the money he lost
The broker closes the position and he can't lose more than he has in the account
Nothing, the broker waits for it to recover
u11l3-10.explanation: European rules limit the damage (close-out at 50 % and no negative balance), but they don't stop you losing what you deposited.
feedback: Nobody pays back CFD losses.
Exactly: retail investors get automatic close-out and negative balance protection, but the loss is already his.
No: in the EU, when margin falls to 50 % of what's required, the broker closes the position and the loss becomes real.

u11l4-3.prompt: How is cashing in a pension plan taxed?
options: As savings income, only on the gain
As employment income, at your marginal rate, on everything you cash in
u11l4-3.explanation: Since contributions got tax relief on the way in, everything is taxed on the way out.

u11l4-4.prompt: What is the general contribution limit for a personal pension plan?
u11l4-4.explanation: You can reach €10,000 in total only by adding contributions to workplace plans.

u11l4-5.prompt: When can you cash in a pension plan? Select all.
options: Contributions that are more than 10 years old
Whenever you like, to go on holiday
u11l4-5.explanation: Outside those cases, the money is locked away.

u11l4-9.prompt: Put the life of a pension plan in order.
options: The money is invested for years without being taxed
Retirement or another cash-in event arrives
You cash it in and it's taxed as employment income
You pay in and reduce your IRPF that year
u11l4-9.explanation: You get tax relief going in, the money grows untaxed and you pay on the way out.

u11l4-11.prompt: Javier is 50, with a high salary and a high marginal IRPF rate. He won't need the money until he retires. He's offered an index plan with low fees. Does it suit him?
options: Yes: he gets tax relief at a high rate, he doesn't need the money and costs are low
Only if the return is guaranteed
No: a pension plan never pays off
u11l4-11.explanation: A plan pays off with a high marginal rate today, low fees and money that won't be needed, and Javier ticks all three. Always ruling it out or demanding guarantees is tempting, but it ignores his situation.
feedback: Good: it's the case where a plan usually pays off, especially if his rate drops when he retires.
An index plan goes up and down with the market: the advantage is in the tax, not in a guarantee.
It depends on each case, and his is one of those that gain most from the tax advantage.

options: No: it's locked away except at retirement, in specific cases or for contributions more than 10 years old
Yes, it works like an account
Yes, by paying a small fee
u11l4-12.explanation: A pension plan can only be cashed in at retirement, in specific cases or for contributions more than 10 years old. Using it as a cushion is tempting because of the tax relief, but a cushion has to be available instantly.
feedback: That's it. For emergencies, an interest-bearing account is better.
No: the money is locked away for years.
It's not about a fee: outside the legal cases, you can't take it out.

u11l5-5.prompt: Which of these products is NOT covered by Spain's deposit guarantee scheme (FGD)?
u11l5-5.explanation: The FGD covers deposits; a money market fund is an investment fund, with its assets kept separate from the management company.

u11l5-9.prompt: In Spain, a money market fund can be transferred to another fund without paying tax.
u11l5-9.explanation: It's an investment fund, so it has the transfer regime.

u11l5-10.prompt: A money market fund can never lose money.
u11l5-10.explanation: Its risk is very low, not zero: it invests in debt that, in extreme cases, can fall in price or not be repaid.

u11l5-11.prompt: An account advertises «4 % APR». The small print: only for 3 months and up to €5,000. You have a €10,000 cushion. What do you do?
options: I put it in shares, they return more
I sign up now: 4 % is a lot
I compare what it would pay me over the whole year with other accounts without those limits
u11l5-11.explanation: Offers with a time or amount limit pay much less than they advertise on all your money. The big number in the ad is tempting, but the terms are what count.
feedback: It's your cushion: it has to be available and not depend on the stock market.
It would only pay that 4 % for a few months and on half your money: the rest of the year, maybe nothing.

u11l5-12.prompt: Where does each pot of money fit best?
options: A monthly contribution for 20 years from now
u11l5-12.explanation: What you'll need soon has to be safe and available, even if it earns little. Over decades, the stock market makes up for its falls; over a few months, there's no time to recover from one.
